svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 3. Traffic fingerprinting results, stated at the right size
svg.desc: An explanation of why published traffic fingerprinting accuracy figures usually overstate real capability. In a closed world test, where the classifier only has to decide which of a small fixed list of sites was visited, accuracy above ninety-five per cent is reported for around five sites, falling below eighty per cent at around twenty-five. In the open world, where a person may visit any site and mostly visits none of the watched ones, the deciding quantity is not accuracy but the false positive rate, because at realistic rates of occurrence a classifier needs orders of magnitude fewer false positives to produce usable results. Measurements using genuine traffic collected at a real exit relay show that synthetic datasets flattered earlier attacks. A panel lists the defences actually deployed, which are narrow: padding that conceals the setup of client-side onion service circuits, and additional restricted guard layers that defend onion services against having their entry relay discovered. A closing band notes that this caution applies equally to a figure cited earlier in this course about encrypted name resolution.
svg.text: Figure 3: Fingerprinting Numbers, and Why Most of Them Are Too Large
Published accuracy figures are real measurements of the wrong situation. Understanding the gap is more useful than memorising any single number.
THE CLOSED WORLD
where most published numbers come from

g.text: The classifier is told the visit was to one of a
small fixed list of sites, and only has to say which.
Above 95 per cent when watching about 5 sites.
Below 80 per cent at about 25 sites.
The number falls as the list grows, and real lists
The measurement is sound. The situation is artificial.

svg.text: THE OPEN WORLD
where people actually browse

g.text: A person may visit any site at all, and almost
always visits none of the ones being watched.
Accuracy stops being the deciding quantity. With
a rare event and a large volume of ordinary traffic,
even a small false positive rate buries every real
Genuine traffic measurements show the gap is large.

svg.text: The specific criticism, which came from measuring real traffic rather than from arguing
Earlier work was evaluated on synthetic datasets: one kind of traffic, simple models of how a person behaves, fixed tooling, front pages only, and no attempt to
reflect how often any given site is actually visited. Attacks tested against traffic genuinely collected at a working exit relay perform substantially worse.
The finding is not that fingerprinting does not work. It is that the published figures describe a task easier than the real one, by a wide margin.
What is actually deployed as a defence
Padding that conceals the setup of client-side onion
service circuits, merged into the software some years
ago and narrow in scope by design.
Extra restricted guard layers that defend an onion
service against having its entry relay discovered.
Note what is not there: general cover traffic.
And this cuts against a figure earlier in this course
Lesson 7.2 cited over ninety per cent accuracy at
identifying sites from encrypted name resolution
traffic, from very short traces.
That figure comes from the same research tradition
and the same caution applies to it.
The claim there should have been stated at this size.
So do not conclude that traffic analysis is solved, in either direction. Conclude that a published accuracy figure describes a laboratory task.
The question to ask of any such number: was the classifier choosing from a short list, and what was its false positive rate at a realistic rate of occurrence?
That is the same discipline this course applies to product claims, applied to research claims, which deserve it just as much.
